HEADLINE: Brazilians vote in presidential election runoff pitting leftist Lula against far-right Bolsonaro
STANDFIRST: "Incumbent president lost in first round to senator and son of convicted ex-president"

THE TWO POLLING-DAY QUOTES — BOTH NEW, BOTH AFTER VOTING
- FLAVIO BOLSONARO, far-right senator and candidate, speaking after voting on Sunday morning at a school in the north zone of Rio de Janeiro: "I think the time has come for real change. Brazil can't take another four years the way things are ... Everyone's life has got worse."
- LUIZ INACIO LULA DA SILVA, President of Brazil, after voting in Sao Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his career began nearly half a century ago, on the pro-Lula demonstrations of the runoff campaign: "What the people have done for me in these past few days is something I can never repay. It is so much generosity, so much affection, so much love. I will be eternally grateful." He added that he was "confident" the people would not choose Bolsonaro, and said he had "never seen anything like" the leftist demonstrations, many emerging organically among young people, that swept the country in his support.

HARD FACTS AND FIGURES
- Lula is 80 and seeking an unprecedented comeback after LOSING the first round. Flavio Bolsonaro is 45, a congressman for more than 20 years "with few bills passed", and is the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
- Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup to overturn his 2022 defeat to Lula. Flavio has promised that if elected he will pardon his father.
- "The gap between them was the narrowest ever recorded in a first round, at less than 2% of the vote."
- Abstention "reached a record high in the first round and disproportionately affects his voters" — Lula's campaign has focused on turnout.
- Electorate: 159 million (see the conflict note in EVE-GEO-AlJazeera-brazil-poll-close-2000gmt.txt).
- Flavio Bolsonaro "is under investigation in two federal police inquiries over alleged corruption and money laundering".
- He has vowed to "change the constitution and re-democratise this country", with a more conservative congress taking office next year.
- Final polls published on Saturday showed Bolsonaro still narrowly ahead (the Guardian's sentence is truncated by its own link markup; do not quote a number from this piece — use the CNT/MDA and Datafolha figures already logged in SUN-GEO-brazil-poll-logistics-and-what-is-not-sourced.txt, attributed to each pollster).

TIMING
- "The result is expected late Sunday evening." NO CLOSING TIME GIVEN. For the 20:00 GMT close see the Al Jazeera file.

NAMED ANALYST AND VOTER QUOTES
- Helcimara de Souza Telles, political scientist: "In the first round, Lula's campaign failed to connect with the population, but now it has been civil society movements that have driven his growth."
- Telles: "Trump wants to 'colonise' all of Latin America in pursuit of its own interests", adding that with right-wing candidates having won all seven presidential elections held in Latin America since Trump began his second term, Brazil is one of the few countries in the region still offering resistance. And: "So a Bolsonaro victory would mean losing Brazil to a model of autocracy backed by the US."
- Nuno Rau, 63, architect and writer, voter: "We're facing two completely different projects for the country. One points towards the end of social rights and the end of democracy itself; on the other side is someone who fought for income distribution and free public education. I may have criticisms of Lula, but there is no way to choose Bolsonaro."
- Aparecida Moreira, 62, lawyer, voting for Bolsonaro mainly for his "iron fist" security policy, including building five "mega-prisons" inspired by those of El Salvador's Nayib Bukele.

CAMPAIGN VIOLENCE — ONE NAMED INCIDENT
- In northern Minas Gerais state, Iara Pimentel, a councillor from Lula's party, was taken to hospital after the motorcade she was travelling in was hit by glass bottles and bricks thrown by Bolsonaro supporters. She said: "It is unacceptable for people to be attacked for expressing their political views." (The Guardian's rendering of the injury itself is broken by its own link markup; do not state the injury type.)

THE RISK LINE
- "Many analysts believe that if Lula overturns his first-round defeat, Bolsonaro could follow his father's example from four years ago and refuse to concede, and that Donald Trump, a longstanding ally of the Bolsonaro clan, could refuse to recognise the result." ANALYST SPECULATION, not a fact. Attribute if used.
